question: to the Commission Arkadiusz Mularczyk (ECR) Subject:
Compliance of ongoing German war-related compensation schemes with EU nondiscrimination law

In the judgments of the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) in the Tas-Hagen (C192/05) and the Nerkowska (C-499/06) cases, the CJEU held that war-victim benefits fall within Member State competence, which must nonetheless be governed in compliance with EU law. Germany continues to pay out this compensation under a law known as Sozialgesetzbuch (Social Code Book) XIV, a successor to the Bundesversorgungsgesetz (Federal War Victims Relief Act), including across borders to other Member States. The authors Karl Heinz Roth and Hartmut Rübner (2022) document that victims of Nazi persecution from Germany received on average EUR 34 628 each, whereas Polish victims received EUR 190.90 – 0.55 % of the amount for German victims – with eligibility partly conditional on the ethnic ‘German language and culture area’ criterion. The same schemes, including under the Bundesversorgungsgesetz, paid out EUR 306 billion (from 1949 to 2000) to recipients the authors classify as the Nazi dictatorship’s military-political personnel (Wehrmacht, WaffenSS and National Socialism officials) – almost six times the total received by all victims. 1.

Can the Commission confirm that Member State competence over war-victim compensation must be exercised in accordance with EU law, including Article 18 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union and Directive 2000/43/EC on equal treatment between persons irrespective of racial or ethnic origin, as regards social protection?
Will the Commission, as guardian of the Treaties, assess whether ethnicity-based eligibility criteria in ongoing German compensation schemes comply with EU law?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.9.2026) In the cases referred to by the Honourable Member, the Court of Justice ruled that, as EU law stands, a benefit intended to compensate civilian victims of war or repression for physical or mental harm which they have suffered falls within the competence of the Member States. However, Member States must exercise that competence in accordance with EU law1. Article 18 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union prohibits discrimination on grounds of nationality for matters that fall within the scope of EU law. In view of the caselaw, there are no indications that the situation referred to by the Honourable Member falls within the scope of EU law. As far as Council Directive 2000/43/EC (‘Racial Equality Directive’)2 is concerned, that Directive prohibits discrimination on the grounds of racial or ethnic origin in certain welldefined fields, including social protection. However, the Racial Equality Directive does not cover discrimination based on nationality3. The Court of Justice clarified that a person’s nationality cannot, in itself, give rise to a presumption of belonging to a particular ethnic group4.
1 Judgment of the Court of Justice of 22 May 2008, Nerkowska, C-499/06, EU:C:2008:300, paragraphs 23-24

and case-law cited. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2000/43/oj/eng. 3 Recital 13 and Article 3(2) of the Racial Equality Directive. 4 Judgment of the Court of Justice of 18 December 2025, Slagelse Almennyttige Boligselskab, Afdeling Schackenborgvænge, C-417/23, ECLI:EU:C:2025:1017, paragraph 81.
